courseTitle: Superpower Relations and the Cold War, 1941–91
eyebrow: EDEXCEL GCSE OPTION P4 (PAPER 2P) • SPECIFICATION CHRONOLOGY • 24 MILESTONES

eras.title: Key Topic 1: The Origins of the Cold War, 1941–58
Key Topic 3: The End of the Cold War, 1970–91

milestones.title: The Grand Alliance & The Tehran Conference
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • Ideological Rivalry & Early Wartime Diplomacy
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Roosevelt and Stalin reach agreement at Tehran in 1943?
milestones.imageCaption: Joseph Stalin, Franklin D. Roosevelt, and Winston Churchill seated at the Tehran Conference in November 1943.
milestones.catalyst: Despite deep ideological hostility between Western **capitalism** and Soviet **communism**, Nazi invasion of the USSR (June 1941) and Pearl Harbor (Dec 1941) forced the USA, Britain, and USSR into a wartime **Grand Alliance**.
milestones.turningPoint: At the **Tehran Conference** (Nov 1943), Roosevelt and Churchill promised Stalin a **Second Front** in France by May 1944; Stalin pledged war against Japan after Hitler's defeat and gained eastern **Poland**.
milestones.impact: Cemented wartime military unity and backing for a post-war **United Nations**, yet rejecting Churchill's Balkan invasion plan left the Red Army poised to liberate and dominate **Eastern Europe**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: As Red Army troops swept across Poland toward Berlin by early 1945, the Big Three reconvened at Yalta and Potsdam to decide defeated Germany's fate.

keyTerms.definition: The 1941–45 wartime coalition of the USA, Britain, and the USSR formed to defeat Nazi Germany and the Axis powers.
The Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied northern France promised at Tehran for May 1944 to relieve pressure on the Red Army.
Rival systems pitting Western multi-party democracy and private enterprise against Soviet one-party rule and state ownership.

milestones.title: Yalta, Potsdam & US Atomic Diplomacy
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • Post-War Division of Germany & Nuclear Monopoly
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What caused relations to sour at Potsdam and after Hiroshima in 1945?
milestones.imageCaption: Clement Attlee, Harry S. Truman, and Joseph Stalin at the Potsdam Conference in July–August 1945.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Allied division of Germany and Berlin into four occupation zones agreed at Yalta and confirmed at Potsdam (1945).
milestones.catalyst: At **Yalta** (Feb 1945), the Big Three agreed on **four occupation zones** in Germany and Berlin plus **free elections** in Eastern Europe, but Roosevelt's death brought anti-communist **Harry S. Truman** to **Potsdam** (July 1945).
milestones.turningPoint: With Nazi Germany defeated and the US **atomic bomb** tested on 16 July 1945, Truman confronted Stalin over Communist control in Poland and reparations before dropping atomic bombs on **Hiroshima** and **Nagasaki** (Aug 1945).
milestones.impact: America's nuclear monopoly failed to intimidate Stalin; instead it poisoned **US–Soviet relations**, accelerated Moscow's own atomic programme (achieved 1949), and hardened Stalin's determination to keep an Eastern European buffer zone.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Mutual suspicion after Hiroshima prompted Washington and Moscow to commission secret diplomatic assessments in 1946 that defined each rival as an existential threat.

keyTerms.definition: The February 1945 Yalta pledge committing the Big Three to hold free democratic elections across nations freed from Nazi rule.
The post-war division of both Germany and Berlin (deep inside the Soviet zone) between the USA, Britain, France, and the USSR.
Compensation in industrial machinery and goods demanded from defeated Germany to rebuild war-devastated Allied economies.

milestones.title: The Long & Novikov Telegrams, Iron Curtain & Satellite States
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • War of Words & Soviet Control in Eastern Europe
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did 1946 telegrams and Soviet satellite states harden superpower distrust?
milestones.imageCaption: Winston Churchill delivering his 'Iron Curtain' speech at Fulton, Missouri on 5 March 1946 alongside President Truman.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The Iron Curtain and creation of Soviet satellite states across Eastern Europe by 1948.
milestones.catalyst: Stalin's February 1946 Bolshoi speech claiming capitalism made war inevitable—alongside rigged elections and secret-police **'salami tactics'** across Poland, Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria—alarmed Western leaders.
milestones.turningPoint: US diplomat **George F. Kennan**'s **Long Telegram** (Feb 1946) urged firm **containment**; Churchill warned at Fulton (March 1946) of an **'Iron Curtain'**; Soviet envoy **Nikolai Novikov**'s September telegram accused Washington of seeking **'world supremacy'**.
milestones.impact: Destroyed remaining wartime goodwill by convincing both capitals the rival superpower was aggressive, locking Eastern Europe into one-party **satellite states** completed by the Feb 1948 Czechoslovak coup.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Convinced by Kennan that Moscow would expand unless firmly checked, Truman moved in March 1947 from verbal warnings to active financial and military containment.

keyTerms.definition: George Kennan's February 1946 cable from Moscow warning that Soviet expansionism had to be met with firm US containment.
Soviet Ambassador Nikolai Novikov's September 1946 report claiming the USA was using atomic and economic might to seek world supremacy.
Eastern European nations formally independent on paper but controlled politically and economically by Moscow as a defensive buffer.

milestones.title: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Cominform & Comecon
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • Containment vs Stalin's Eastern Counter-Bloc
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did US containment and Stalin's counter-bodies split Europe into two blocs?
milestones.imageCaption: West German reconstruction sign ('Hier hilft der Marshallplan') advertising European Recovery Program aid in 1948.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Rival Marshall Plan recipients in Western Europe versus Cominform and Comecon states in the Soviet bloc.
milestones.catalyst: Post-war hunger threatened Communist gains in Western Europe, and in February 1947 bankrupt Britain announced it could no longer fund royalist forces in the **Greek Civil War** or protect **Turkey**.
milestones.turningPoint: Truman's **Truman Doctrine** (March 1947) sent **$400m** to Greece and Turkey to contain communism, backed by over **$13bn** in **Marshall Plan** recovery aid for 16 Western nations; Stalin answered with **Cominform** (Sept 1947) and **Comecon** (Jan 1949).
milestones.impact: Ended US peacetime isolationism and rebuilt Western Europe, while Stalin's condemnation of **'dollar imperialism'** barred satellites from Marshall Aid and sealed Europe's division into two rival ideological and economic camps.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Pumping Marshall Plan aid and a new Western currency into western Germany provoked Stalin's first direct military confrontation with the West over Berlin in June 1948.

keyTerms.definition: President Truman's March 1947 pledge of US military and financial aid to help free nations resist Communist takeover.
The 1947–52 US European Recovery Program supplying over $13bn ($17bn total) to rebuild 16 Western European economies.
Stalin's ideological bureau (Sept 1947) and economic council (Jan 1949) enforcing Moscow's political and trade control over satellite states.

milestones.title: The Berlin Blockade & The Allied Airlift
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • The First Berlin Crisis & Division of Germany
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Truman and Britain sustain West Berlin without triggering war?
milestones.imageCaption: West Berlin children watching an American C-54 Skymaster approach Tempelhof Airport during the 1948–49 Berlin Airlift.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Four occupation zones of Germany and the three 20-mile Allied air corridors supplying blockaded West Berlin.
milestones.catalyst: Britain, France, and the USA merged their German zones into **Bizonia** and **Trizonia** and introduced the **Deutschmark** in June 1948, alarming Stalin over a reviving capitalist West Germany and an affluent **West Berlin** inside his zone.
milestones.turningPoint: On 24 June 1948 Stalin blocked all road, rail, and canal routes into West Berlin; the Allies answered with an 11-month **Berlin Airlift** (**Operation Vittles** / Plainfare), flying **275,000+ flights** until Stalin lifted the siege on 12 May 1949.
milestones.impact: Proved **containment** worked peacefully while portraying Stalin as a ruthless aggressor; destroyed any hope of a united Germany, splitting it into **West Germany (FRG, May 1949)** and **East Germany (GDR, Oct 1949)**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Stalin's blockade convinced Western democracies they needed a permanent military shield, triggering rival nuclear-armed alliances across Europe.

keyTerms.definition: The 1947–48 economic merger of the British, American, and French occupation zones of western Germany.
The 11-month Allied aerial lifeline delivering up to 8,000–13,000 tons of coal and food daily along three air corridors to 2.1 million West Berliners.
The capitalist Federal Republic of Germany (West, May 1949) and Communist German Democratic Republic (East, October 1949).

milestones.title: Formation of NATO, The Nuclear Arms Race & The Warsaw Pact
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2–1.3 • Rival Military Alliances & Thermonuclear Escalation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: In what ways did NATO, the arms race, and the Warsaw Pact intensify rivalry by 1955?
milestones.imageCaption: President Harry S. Truman signing the North Atlantic Treaty in the Oval Office in April 1949.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Armed division of Europe between NATO (1949, joined by FRG in 1955) and the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact (May 1955).
milestones.catalyst: Shaken by the 1948 Czech coup and Berlin Blockade, Western Europe sought US military protection, while Moscow tested its first **atomic bomb** in August 1949 to break America's nuclear monopoly.
milestones.turningPoint: Twelve Western nations signed **NATO** (4 April 1949) under **Article 5** collective defence; both superpowers developed **hydrogen bombs** (USA 1952, USSR 1953); when West Germany joined NATO in May 1955, **Nikita Khrushchev** formed the **Warsaw Pact**.
milestones.impact: Committed the USA permanently to European defence, locked Europe into two opposing military blocs under unified commands, and shifted warfare toward thermonuclear deterrence.
milestones.bridgeToNext: After Stalin's death, Khrushchev's February 1956 'Secret Speech' raised hopes of reform inside the new Warsaw Pact—igniting open revolt in Budapest.

keyTerms.definition: The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation founded in April 1949, binding the USA, Canada, and Western Europe under Article 5 collective security.
Thermonuclear weapon roughly 1,000 times stronger than Hiroshima, tested by the USA in 1952 and the USSR in 1953.
The May 1955 military alliance uniting the USSR and seven Eastern European satellite states under Soviet command after West Germany joined NATO.

milestones.title: Khrushchev’s ‘Secret Speech’ & Imre Nagy’s Reforms in Hungary
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 • Causes & Events of the 1956 Hungarian Uprising
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did discontent explode across Hungary in October 1956?
milestones.imageCaption: Budapest demonstrators beside the toppled bronze statue of Joseph Stalin during the October 1956 Hungarian Uprising.
milestones.catalyst: Years of **Mátyás Rákosi**'s **ÁVH** secret-police terror, censorship, and falling **Comecon** living standards collided with **Khrushchev**'s February 1956 **'Secret Speech'** promising de-Stalinisation.
milestones.turningPoint: After Budapest student protests toppled Stalin's statue on 23 October 1956, new Prime Minister **Imre Nagy** abolished the ÁVH, promised multi-party **free elections**, and on **1 November** announced Hungary would leave the **Warsaw Pact**.
milestones.impact: Tested the limits of Khrushchev's 'peaceful coexistence': Moscow could tolerate cautious domestic reform, but neutral withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact threatened to unravel the entire Soviet buffer zone.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Fearing Poland and East Germany would copy Hungarian neutrality—and pressured by Kremlin hardliners and Mao—Khrushchev ordered tanks back into Budapest within 72 hours.

keyTerms.definition: Khrushchev's policy from his February 1956 Secret Speech denouncing Stalin's purges while maintaining one-party Communist control.
Hungary's hated Communist secret police under Mátyás Rákosi, responsible for mass arrests, censorship, and executions.
Imre Nagy's fatal 1 November 1956 declaration withdrawing Hungary from the Warsaw Pact and appealing for UN protection.

milestones.title: Operation Whirlwind, Kádár’s Repression & Western Inaction
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 • Khrushchev's Response & International Reaction
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Khrushchev crush Hungary—and why did the USA take no military action?
milestones.imageCaption: A Soviet tank deployed in Budapest during November 1956 as Operation Whirlwind crushed the Hungarian Uprising.
milestones.catalyst: Nagy's 1 November withdrawal from the **Warsaw Pact** crossed Moscow's red line while Britain and France distracted world attention by invading Egypt in the simultaneous **Suez Crisis**.
milestones.turningPoint: At dawn on **4 November 1956**, Khrushchev sent **1,000+ Soviet tanks** into Budapest (**Operation Whirlwind**), killing ~2,500 Hungarians, driving **200,000 refugees** into Austria, installing **János Kádár**, and executing Nagy in June 1958.
milestones.impact: Tightened Soviet iron discipline across the Warsaw Pact while exposing US 'rollback' talk as hollow: **Eisenhower** sent humanitarian aid and UN protests but risked no nuclear war inside Moscow's sphere.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Emboldened by Western military restraint over Hungary and the 1957 Sputnik ICBM launch, Khrushchev turned in November 1958 to end the refugee drain through West Berlin.

keyTerms.definition: The 4 November 1956 Soviet invasion using over 1,000 tanks to crush Nagy's government in Budapest.
Pro-Soviet Hungarian leader installed by Khrushchev to enforce a 15-point programme restoring one-party rule and Warsaw Pact loyalty.
The simultaneous October–November 1956 Anglo-French-Israeli invasion of Egypt that split NATO and blunted Western condemnation of Moscow.

milestones.title: Refugee Brain Drain, Berlin Ultimatum & The U-2 Summit Wreck
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Berlin Refugee Crisis & 1959–60 Summit Diplomacy
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Khrushchev issue his 1958 Berlin Ultimatum and walk out of Paris in 1960?
milestones.imageCaption: Captured CIA pilot Francis Gary Powers in Moscow after a Soviet missile downed his U-2 spy plane on 1 May 1960.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Divided Berlin showing Western air corridors and the pre-1961 East-to-West refugee escape route.
milestones.catalyst: Prosperous **West Berlin** acted as an escape hatch for **2.7–3 million** East Germans fleeing low wages and **Stasi** rule under Walter Ulbricht—a crippling **'brain drain'** of young doctors, engineers, and skilled workers.
milestones.turningPoint: Khrushchev's **27 November 1958 Berlin Ultimatum** gave Western powers six months to leave West Berlin; **Geneva** and **Camp David** (1959) eased tension until a Soviet missile downed **Gary Powers's U-2 spy plane** (1 May 1960), wrecking the **Paris Summit**.
milestones.impact: Destroyed Eisenhower-Khrushchev trust, left Berlin's status unresolved, and accelerated the East German refugee flood as citizens feared the border would soon shut.
milestones.bridgeToNext: As Berlin diplomacy froze in 1960, superpower rivalry simultaneously exploded just 90 miles off Florida following Fidel Castro's revolution in Cuba.

keyTerms.definition: The exodus of roughly 2.7–3 million East Germans—especially skilled professionals—into West Germany via West Berlin between 1949 and 1961.
Khrushchev's November 1958 six-month demand for Western troops to leave West Berlin and turn it into a demilitarised 'free city'.
The downing of CIA pilot Francis Gary Powers over the USSR on 1 May 1960, causing Khrushchev to walk out of the Paris Summit when Eisenhower refused to apologise.

milestones.title: The Cuban Revolution, Soviet Alignment & The Bay of Pigs
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • US Refusal to Recognise Castro & Failed Invasion
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did US hostility and the April 1961 Bay of Pigs fiasco push Cuba into Moscow's arms?
milestones.imageCaption: Captured CIA-backed Brigade 2506 exile prisoners in Cuba after Castro's forces crushed the April 1961 Bay of Pigs landing.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Strategic proximity of Cuba (90 miles from Florida) and Soviet missile ranges across the United States.
milestones.catalyst: After **Fidel Castro** toppled US-backed dictator Batista in **January 1959** and nationalised US-owned sugar and oil assets, Washington's refusal to recognise Castro's government, sugar cuts, and **October 1960 trade embargo** pushed Havana to trade sugar for Soviet oil and arms.
milestones.turningPoint: On **17 April 1961**, new President **John F. Kennedy** sent **1,400** CIA-trained Cuban exiles (**Brigade 2506**) ashore at the **Bay of Pigs** without US air cover; **20,000** Cuban troops crushed the landing within 72 hours.
milestones.impact: Humiliated Kennedy internationally, rallied Cubans behind Castro—who declared Cuba **Communist** in December 1961—and prompted Castro to ask Khrushchev for Soviet military protection against a direct US invasion.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Convinced after the Bay of Pigs fiasco that young President Kennedy was weak and indecisive, Khrushchev immediately tried to bully him over Berlin at Vienna in June 1961.

keyTerms.definition: Fidel Castro and Che Guevara's January 1959 overthrow of pro-US dictator Fulgencio Batista 90 miles south of Florida.
Economic sanctions imposed by Eisenhower in October 1960 banning US exports to Cuba and driving Castro into Soviet trade dependence.
Failed April 1961 CIA-backed landing of 1,400 Brigade 2506 Cuban exiles defeated by Castro's army in three days.

milestones.title: Vienna Summit, Construction of the Berlin Wall & Checkpoint Charlie
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2–2.3 • Crisis in Berlin & Concrete Division (1961)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What caused East Germany to build the Berlin Wall in August 1961?
milestones.imageCaption: East German crews guarded by armed border troops erecting concrete blocks behind barbed wire along the Berlin Wall in August 1961.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The 1961 Berlin Wall encircling West Berlin inside the GDR and Allied crossing at Checkpoint Charlie.
milestones.catalyst: At the **June 1961 Vienna Summit**, Khrushchev renewed his six-month Berlin Ultimatum; Kennedy refused to yield, adding **$3.2bn** to US defence spending as **over 30,000** East Germans fled westward in July 1961 alone.
milestones.turningPoint: Before dawn on **13 August 1961**, East German troops sealed West Berlin with barbed wire and built a **3.6m concrete Berlin Wall** and mined **'Death Strip'**; in October, US and Soviet tanks faced off for 18 hours at **Checkpoint Charlie**.
milestones.impact: Stopped the GDR's refugee **brain drain** and removed Berlin as a flashpoint for war (*'a wall is a hell of a lot better than a war'*), yet handed the West a lasting propaganda triumph as guards shot escapers like **Peter Fechter** (1962).
milestones.bridgeToNext: With Berlin sealed in concrete, Khrushchev secretly gambled in May 1962 on shipping nuclear missiles to Cuba—sparking the Cold War's closest brush with nuclear war.

keyTerms.definition: Tense June 1961 meeting where Khrushchev reissued his six-month Berlin Ultimatum to test new US President John F. Kennedy.
Fortified concrete barrier, watchtowers, and 'Death Strip' erected around West Berlin from 13 August 1961 to halt East German escapes.
Main Allied sector crossing in Berlin where American and Soviet tanks stood 100 metres apart for 18 hours on 27 October 1961.

milestones.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis: U-2 Discovery, Quarantine & Secret Deal
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Events of the Cuban Missile Crisis (Oct 1962)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Kennedy and Khrushchev step back from nuclear war in October 1962?
milestones.imageCaption: Declassified USAF U-2 reconnaissance photograph revealing Soviet medium-range missile launch sites at San Cristóbal, Cuba, 14 October 1962.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Soviet SS-4 and SS-5 nuclear strike radii from Cuba alongside the 500-mile US Navy quarantine line.
milestones.catalyst: To defend Communist Cuba and counter **US Jupiter missiles in Turkey**, Khrushchev secretly shipped medium-range nuclear missiles to Cuba; on **14 October 1962**, a US **U-2** spy plane photographed launch sites at San Cristóbal.
milestones.turningPoint: Advised by **ExComm**, Kennedy ordered a **500-mile naval quarantine** on 22 October (**DEFCON 2**); Soviet ships turned back on 24 October, and on **28 October** Khrushchev agreed to remove Cuban missiles for a public US **non-invasion pledge** and secret withdrawal of Turkish missiles.
milestones.impact: Averted nuclear annihilation at the eleventh hour, boosted Kennedy's authority enormously, and fatally damaged Khrushchev's prestige inside the Kremlin because the Turkish missile concession remained secret—contributing to his 1964 removal.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Terrified by how close Thirteen Days came to nuclear catastrophe, both superpowers moved rapidly in 1963 to build direct communication links and nuclear arms treaties.

keyTerms.definition: President Kennedy's secret Executive Committee of the National Security Council convened to manage the Thirteen Days crisis.
The 500-mile US Navy zone around Cuba announced on 22 October 1962 to block Soviet missile shipments without declaring formal war.
Robert Kennedy's secret 27 October assurance to Soviet envoy Dobrynin that obsolete US Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be removed quietly.

milestones.title: Kennedy in Berlin, The Hotline & Early Arms Control Treaties
milestones.specTag: KT 2.3 • Consequences of Berlin & Cuba; Attempts at Arms Control
milestones.enquiryQuestion: In what ways did the Berlin and Cuba crises lead to safer superpower rules by 1968?
milestones.imageCaption: President John F. Kennedy ratifying the Limited Test Ban Treaty at the White House in October 1963.
milestones.catalyst: Both the 1961 Berlin standoff and the October 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis proved that slow diplomatic messages and unchecked nuclear proliferation risked accidental **Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)**.
milestones.turningPoint: On 26 June 1963 Kennedy proclaimed **'Ich bin ein Berliner'** in West Berlin while opening the **Moscow–Washington 'hotline'**; sustained **attempts at arms control** produced the **Limited Test Ban Treaty (Aug 1963)**, **Outer Space Treaty (1967)**, and **Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968)**.
milestones.impact: Stabilised **US–Soviet relations** with practical crisis guardrails and curbed atmospheric fallout and nuclear spread, paving the way for 1970s Détente even as Moscow replaced Khrushchev with **Leonid Brezhnev** (1964).
milestones.bridgeToNext: While Washington and Moscow stabilised nuclear rules, economic stagnation and censorship inside Czechoslovakia sparked a bold Communist reform movement in January 1968.

keyTerms.definition: Direct teletype communication link between the Kremlin and the White House enabling rapid leader-to-leader contact in crises.
August 1963 pact signed by the USA, USSR, and Britain banning nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere, outer space, and underwater.
Treaties barring nuclear weapons from space (1967) and committing nuclear states not to share atomic technology with non-nuclear nations (1968).

milestones.title: Alexander Dubček’s Action Programme & The Prague Spring
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Opposition in Czechoslovakia to Soviet Control
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Dubček's 1968 'Prague Spring' reforms alarm Moscow so deeply?
milestones.imageCaption: Alexander Dubček, Czechoslovak Communist First Secretary who launched 'Socialism with a human face' in spring 1968.
milestones.catalyst: Hardline Stalinist **Antonín Novotný**'s **StB** secret-police censorship, Slovak grievances, and **Comecon**-driven economic decline provoked 1967 student protests, bringing reformist **Alexander Dubček** to power in January 1968.
milestones.turningPoint: Dubček's April 1968 ***Action Programme*** launched the **Prague Spring** (**'Socialism with a human face'**), ending press censorship, curbing StB arrests, allowing Western travel, and decentralising trade while pledging loyalty to the **Warsaw Pact**.
milestones.impact: Uncensored debate and Ludvík Vaculík's June ***Two Thousand Words*** manifesto terrified **Leonid Brezhnev**, East Germany's Ulbricht, and Poland's Gomułka that democratic reform would infect neighbouring satellites and split the Warsaw Pact.
milestones.bridgeToNext: After the July Warsaw Letter and tense Čierna and Bratislava summits failed to make Dubček reimpose censorship, Brezhnev ordered massive military intervention.

keyTerms.definition: Brief period of political, cultural, and economic liberalisation in Czechoslovakia from January to August 1968 under Alexander Dubček.
Dubček's slogan aiming to make Communist rule popular by combining state socialism and Warsaw Pact loyalty with free speech.
April 1968 Czechoslovak Communist manifesto abolishing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and introducing market decentralisation.

milestones.title: The Warsaw Pact Invasion of Czechoslovakia & Moscow Protocol
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Re-Establishment of Soviet Control in Prague
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Warsaw Pact forces seize Czechoslovakia and crush the Prague Spring?
milestones.imageCaption: Unarmed Prague demonstrators carrying the Czechoslovak flag past Soviet tanks during the August 1968 Warsaw Pact invasion.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Multi-front invasion of Czechoslovakia by 500,000 Soviet, Polish, Hungarian, and Bulgarian troops (20–21 Aug 1968).
milestones.catalyst: Dubček's warm Prague welcome for independent Communist leaders **Tito** (Yugoslavia) and **Ceaușescu** (Romania) in August 1968 convinced Moscow that Czechoslovakia was slipping out of Kremlin control.
milestones.turningPoint: On **20–21 August 1968**, **500,000 Warsaw Pact troops** invaded Czechoslovakia; Dubček urged peaceful **passive resistance** (keeping deaths below 100), before being arrested and forced to sign the **Moscow Protocol** on 26 August.
milestones.impact: Ended the Prague Spring, stationed Red Army troops permanently in Czechoslovakia, prompted student **Jan Palach**'s January 1969 protest suicide, and installed hardliner **Gustáv Husák** (April 1969) to purge ~500,000 party reformers under **'normalisation'**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To justify invading a loyal ally that had never left the Warsaw Pact, Brezhnev proclaimed a sweeping new doctrine of limited socialist sovereignty that autumn.

keyTerms.definition: Peaceful Czechoslovak defiance in August 1968—removing road signs, arguing with tank crews, and running secret radio broadcasts.
Coerced 26 August 1968 pact signed by arrested Prague leaders restoring censorship, banning opposition clubs, and accepting Soviet garrisons.
Gustáv Husák's hardline rule from April 1969 reversing Prague Spring reforms and restoring strict StB police control.

milestones.title: The Brezhnev Doctrine, Western Restraint & Splits in World Communism
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2–2.3 • Brezhnev Doctrine & International Reaction
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Brezhnev Doctrine lock Eastern Europe yet fracture world Communism?
milestones.imageCaption: Soviet General Secretary Leonid Brezhnev clasping hands with East German leader Erich Honecker.
milestones.catalyst: Moscow needed an ideological rule to stop any future Eastern European reform movement threatening Communist monopoly, while Washington was bogged down with **500,000 US troops in Vietnam**.
milestones.turningPoint: Outlined in *Pravda* (Sept 1968) and Warsaw (Nov 1968), the **Brezhnev Doctrine** declared that if **one-party Communist rule** or Warsaw Pact unity was threatened anywhere, all socialist states had a duty to intervene militarily.
milestones.impact: Froze Eastern European satellites under Kremlin obedience until 1989 while US action stopped at UN condemnation (vetoed by Moscow); however, **Romania**, **Yugoslavia**, **China**, and Western **Eurocommunist** parties angrily condemned Soviet tanks.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With European spheres frozen—and both superpowers strained by Vietnam costs, Sino-Soviet tension, and nuclear parity—Nixon and Brezhnev pivoted toward Détente in the early 1970s.

keyTerms.definition: Autumn 1968 Soviet principle asserting Warsaw Pact states had a collective right and duty to crush any threat to one-party Communist rule.
Movement among French and Italian Communist Parties rejecting Moscow's authority in favour of independent democratic politics after Prague 1968.

milestones.title: Pressures for Détente & The May 1972 SALT 1 Moscow Summit
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Détente & Strategic Arms Limitation (SALT 1)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Nixon and Brezhnev pursue Détente and sign SALT 1 in May 1972?
milestones.imageCaption: US President Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signing the SALT 1 accords in Moscow, 26 May 1972.
milestones.catalyst: America faced **$150bn+ Vietnam War** costs, **58,000** deaths, and domestic unrest, while Brezhnev needed US grain, Western technology, and diplomatic security after the **Sino-Soviet split** and Nixon's Feb 1972 China visit.
milestones.turningPoint: At the **Moscow Summit (26 May 1972)**, Nixon and Brezhnev signed **SALT 1**: the **ABM Treaty** capped anti-missile shields at two sites each, the **Interim Agreement** froze ICBM/SLBM launchers for five years, and **Basic Principles** pledged restraint.
milestones.impact: Marked the first formal superpower nuclear arms ceiling and opened major grain trade, though **SALT 1** failed to ban **MIRVs** (multiple warheads per missile), allowing total warhead stockpiles to keep climbing.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Building on Moscow's diplomatic momentum, 35 nations gathered in 1975 to widen Détente across space cooperation, European borders, and human rights.

keyTerms.definition: The 1970s relaxation of superpower Cold War tension managed through regular summits, arms treaties, and East–West trade.
First Strategic Arms Limitation agreements combining the ABM Treaty, a five-year freeze on ICBM/SLBM launchers, and Basic Principles.
Multiple Independently Targetable Re-entry Vehicle—single missiles carrying several nuclear warheads, left unrestricted by SALT 1.

milestones.title: Apollo–Soyuz Space Handshake & The Three Baskets of Helsinki
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • High Point & Hidden Contradictions of Détente
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the August 1975 Helsinki Accords both reward and embarrass the USSR?
milestones.imageCaption: President Gerald Ford and Henry Kissinger conferring with Leonid Brezhnev during the Helsinki Summit in August 1975.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The 35 signatory states and Three Baskets of the August 1975 Helsinki Accords.
milestones.catalyst: Expanding US–Soviet summits (1973–74) and joint scientific exchanges culminated on **17 July 1975** when American **Apollo** and Soviet **Soyuz** spacecraft docked in orbit.
milestones.turningPoint: In **August 1975**, US President **Gerald Ford**, **Brezhnev**, Canada, and 32 European states signed the **Helsinki Accords** across three Baskets: **Basket 1** (inviolable post-1945 borders & GDR recognition), **Basket 2** (trade/science), and **Basket 3** (**human rights**).
milestones.impact: Represented Détente's high-water mark by recognising Soviet-bloc borders, yet **Basket 3** inspired **Helsinki Watch** groups and Czech **Charter 77** dissidents to expose Communist repression—fuelling US human-rights criticism under Jimmy Carter.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Carter's human-rights diplomacy, Soviet SS-20 missiles, and Third World rivalries strained Détente until Soviet tanks rolled into Afghanistan in December 1979.

keyTerms.definition: Joint US–Soviet orbital mission where commander Thomas Stafford and cosmonaut Alexei Leonov shook hands in space.
Landmark 35-nation declaration agreeing European borders (Basket 1), economic/scientific cooperation (Basket 2), and human rights (Basket 3).
Helsinki pledge to protect free speech, religion, and movement, used by Soviet-bloc dissidents to hold Moscow publicly accountable.

milestones.title: Vienna SALT 2 Signing & The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1–3.2 • Collapse of Détente (Dec 1979)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Brezhnev order the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979?
milestones.imageCaption: Soviet airborne soldiers boarding a Mil Mi-8 transport helicopter during operations in Afghanistan.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: December 1979 Soviet invasion routes into Afghanistan and proximity to the Persian Gulf and Soviet Central Asia.
milestones.catalyst: Although **Jimmy Carter** and **Brezhnev** signed **SALT 2** in June 1979 (capping strategic launchers at 2,400), Islamic **Mujahideen** rebels threatened Kabul's Communist PDPA regime after **Hafizullah Amin** seized power next to revolutionary Iran.
milestones.turningPoint: Fearing Islamic fundamentalism spreading to **30 million** Soviet Muslims and suspecting Amin of US ties, Brezhnev invaded **Afghanistan** on **24–27 December 1979**, killing Amin and installing pro-Moscow **Babrak Karmal**.
milestones.impact: Killed **Détente** overnight, prompted Carter to withdraw **SALT 2** from the US Senate in January 1980, and trapped the USSR in a bleeding ten-year guerrilla war costing **$8bn a year** and **15,000 Soviet dead**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Viewing Soviet troops near the Persian Gulf as the gravest threat to peace since 1945, President Carter launched sweeping military, economic, and sporting sanctions in 1980.

keyTerms.definition: Vienna arms treaty capping strategic nuclear launchers at 2,400 and limiting MIRVs; never ratified after Moscow invaded Afghanistan.
Islamic guerrilla fighters waging holy war against Kabul's Communist government and occupying Red Army forces (1979–89).
Pro-Soviet Afghan Communist leader installed in Kabul after Soviet forces stormed the palace and killed Hafizullah Amin in December 1979.

milestones.title: The Carter Doctrine, Sanctions & The 1980 Moscow Olympic Boycott
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2 • US Retaliation Over Afghanistan
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Jimmy Carter retaliate against the USSR across diplomacy, trade, and sport in 1980?
milestones.imageCaption: Central Lenin Stadium in Moscow during the 1980 Summer Olympics, boycotted by over 60 US-led nations.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Over 60 nations (highlighted in blue) joining the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Summer Olympics.
milestones.catalyst: Brezhnev refused President Carter's February 1980 ultimatum to withdraw Soviet troops from **Afghanistan**, raising Western fears that Soviet armour could push south toward **Persian Gulf** oil supplies.
milestones.turningPoint: In **January 1980** Carter proclaimed the **Carter Doctrine** pledging US military force to defend the Persian Gulf, halted grain and high-tech exports, armed the Mujahideen (**Operation Cyclone**), and led **60+ nations** to boycott the **1980 Moscow Olympics**.
milestones.impact: Publicly humiliated the Kremlin's multi-billion-rouble Olympic showcase, severed Détente's trade and grain lifelines, and reopened full-scale superpower confrontation.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Believing even Carter's sanctions were too soft, newly elected US President Ronald Reagan escalated ideological and high-tech military pressure from January 1981.

keyTerms.definition: Pledge that the USA would use military force if needed to block any outside power gaining control of the oil-rich Persian Gulf.
Covert CIA programme channelling money and weapons through Pakistan to arm Afghan Mujahideen fighters against Soviet troops.
US-led sporting protest by over 60 countries refusing to attend the 1980 Summer Olympics until Soviet forces left Afghanistan.

milestones.title: Reagan’s ‘Second Cold War’, ‘Evil Empire’, Star Wars (SDI) & 1984 LA Boycott
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2 • Rearmament, SDI & Frozen Relations
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Ronald Reagan's 'Second Cold War' and SDI alarm the Kremlin so deeply?
milestones.imageCaption: 1984 US Department of Defense concept illustration of orbiting laser satellites for Reagan's Strategic Defence Initiative ('Star Wars').
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Global Cold War alignments during the renewed superpower confrontation of the early 1980s.
milestones.catalyst: Dismissing Détente as a *'one-way street'*, President **Ronald Reagan** (1981) resolved to negotiate only from overwhelming military and technological strength against an ageing Kremlin leadership.
milestones.turningPoint: Reagan launched a **$1 trillion** defence build-up (Trident, B-1 bombers, Pershing II/Cruise missiles), branded the USSR an **'Evil Empire'** (8 March 1983), unveiled **SDI ('Star Wars')** laser satellites (23 March 1983), and faced a retaliatory **14-nation Soviet boycott of the 1984 LA Olympics**.
milestones.impact: Threatened **MAD** by promising an American space shield against Soviet ICBMs; lagging far behind in microchips and computers, Moscow knew matching **SDI** would bankrupt its stagnant command economy.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Economic exhaustion, Afghan casualties, and SDI pressure convinced dynamic new Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev in March 1985 that survival required radical reform and disarmament.

keyTerms.definition: Period of intense superpower confrontation marked by Afghanistan, collapsed arms talks, US rearmament, and 'Evil Empire' rhetoric.
Reagan's March 1983 'Star Wars' plan for space-based laser satellites to intercept Soviet ICBMs in flight.
Retaliatory boycott of the 1984 Los Angeles Summer Olympics by the USSR and 14 Eastern Bloc allies.

milestones.title: Gorbachev’s ‘New Thinking’, Geneva, Reykjavik & The December 1987 INF Treaty
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2–3.3 • Perestroika, Glasnost & Historic Disarmament
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Reagan and Gorbachev move from SDI deadlock to the 1987 INF Treaty?
milestones.imageCaption: Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan signing the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty at the White House, 8 December 1987.
milestones.catalyst: With military spending consuming **~25% of Soviet GDP**, food queues growing, and the **April 1986 Chernobyl** nuclear disaster exposing decay, **Mikhail Gorbachev** needed deep arms cuts to fund domestic reform.
milestones.turningPoint: Gorbachev launched **Perestroika** (restructuring) and **Glasnost** (openness), built rapport with Reagan at **Geneva (Nov 1985)** and **Reykjavik (Oct 1986)**, uncoupled talks from SDI, and signed the **INF Treaty** in Washington (**8 Dec 1987**).
milestones.impact: Eliminated an entire class of US and Soviet land-based missiles (**500–5,500 km range**, destroying **2,600+ SS-20, Pershing II, and Cruise missiles**) with on-site inspections—transforming superpower rivalry into genuine partnership.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Determined to slash military costs further, Gorbachev announced at the UN in December 1988 that Soviet tanks would no longer prop up unpopular Eastern European regimes.

keyTerms.definition: Gorbachev's twin reforms restructuring the stagnant Soviet economy while relaxing censorship and freeing dissidents to save socialism.
Iceland summit where Reagan and Gorbachev nearly abolished ballistic missiles before talks stalled over Reagan's refusal to scrap SDI.
Landmark Washington treaty abolishing all US and Soviet intermediate-range (500–5,500 km) land-based missiles under strict inspection.

milestones.title: Loosening the Soviet Grip, Eastern Bloc Revolutions & Fall of the Berlin Wall
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 • Gorbachev's Impact on Eastern Europe & Fall of the Wall
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Gorbachev's 'Sinatra Doctrine' trigger the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989?
milestones.imageCaption: East and West Berliners celebrating atop the Berlin Wall in front of the Brandenburg Gate in November 1989.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The 1989 revolutions across Eastern Europe, fall of the Berlin Wall, and dissolution of the Soviet bloc.
milestones.catalyst: Gorbachev's December 1988 UN speech cutting **500,000 troops**, February 1989 Afghan withdrawal, and abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine (**'Sinatra Doctrine'**) initiated **the loosening Soviet grip on Eastern Europe**.
milestones.turningPoint: **Solidarity** won Poland's June 1989 elections, Hungary opened its Austrian border, **70,000+** protested in Leipzig, and on **9 November 1989** fumbled GDR travel rules by **Günter Schabowski** led crowds to tear open the **Berlin Wall**.
milestones.impact: Shattered the supreme physical symbol of Cold War division without a shot fired, triggering Czechoslovakia's peaceful **Velvet Revolution**, Romania's overthrow of Ceaușescu, and **German reunification** inside NATO (3 Oct 1990).
milestones.bridgeToNext: Losing Eastern Europe inspired independence movements inside the USSR's own republics and enraged Kremlin hardliners into staging a desperate coup against Gorbachev.

keyTerms.definition: Soviet policy replacing the Brezhnev Doctrine by allowing Warsaw Pact states to choose their own political path without Red Army intervention.
Lech Wałęsa's independent Polish trade union that won 99 of 100 Senate seats in June 1989 to form the bloc's first non-communist government.
Opening of East Berlin border checkpoints on the night of 9 November 1989 after mass protests and Schabowski's televised briefing.

milestones.title: Malta Summit, Dissolution of the Warsaw Pact, August Coup & Collapse of the USSR
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 • End of the Warsaw Pact & Collapse of the Soviet Union
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Warsaw Pact and the Soviet Union itself dissolve in 1991?
milestones.imageCaption: Leaders of Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia (Boris Yeltsin, right) signing the Belavezha Accords establishing the CIS on 8 December 1991.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Dissolution of the Warsaw Pact (July 1991) and breakup of the USSR into 15 independent republics (December 1991).
milestones.catalyst: After Gorbachev and **George H. W. Bush** declared the Cold War over at **Malta (Dec 1989)**, newly democratic satellites dissolved the **Warsaw Pact (1 July 1991)** while **Perestroika** shortages and **Glasnost** fuelled Baltic nationalism.
milestones.turningPoint: On **19–21 August 1991**, the hardline Communist **Gang of Eight** staged a Moscow coup to block Gorbachev's New Union Treaty; Russian President **Boris Yeltsin** defeated the coup, formed the **CIS** (Dec 1991), and **Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991**.
milestones.impact: Lowered the Soviet flag over the Kremlin forever, split the USSR into **15 independent states**, confirmed the irreversible end of the Warsaw Pact, and left the **United States** as the world's sole superpower after fifty years of rivalry.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Fifty years after the wartime Grand Alliance of 1941, the ideological, nuclear, and territorial division of Europe and the Cold War had come to a peaceful end.

keyTerms.definition: Shipboard summit where Mikhail Gorbachev and US President George H. W. Bush formally declared the Cold War over.
Failed August 1991 Moscow coup by Communist Party and KGB hardliners defeated by Boris Yeltsin's popular resistance.
Loose association (CIS) formed in December 1991 by Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and eight former Soviet republics replacing the dissolved USSR.
